blocks.content: The Supreme Court of India severely criticized the agency by observing that the CBI has become a caged parrot speaking in its master's voice.

rows: A standing consent given by a state allowing CBI to seamlessly register and investigate cases in that state.
Case-by-case approval required from the state government before registering an investigation.
CBI cannot register fresh cases in that state without explicit permission for each case.
CBI must apply to the state government separately for every single case it seeks to investigate.
Investigations started prior to withdrawal of consent remain unaffected and can continue.
Applies strictly to new cases; old ongoing investigations retain validity.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The CBI is not a statutory body; it derives its investigating powers from the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946.
Under Section 6 of the DSPE Act, the CBI requires the prior consent of the concerned state government to conduct investigations within that state's jurisdiction.
In 2013, the Supreme Court of India famously characterized the CBI as a 'caged parrot speaking in its master's voice' due to excessive political executive interference.
The agency faces structural dependence, relies heavily on personnel on deputation from state police forces, and suffers from manpower shortages.
Anti-corruption investigations by the CBI are supervised by the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), whereas overall administrative control rests with the Ministry of Personnel.
CBI is NOT created by an Act of Parliament; it was set up by a resolution of the Ministry of Home Affairs and derives power from the DSPE Act, 1946.
Section 6 of the DSPE Act makes state government consent mandatory for CBI operations in any state.
Superintendence over CBI regarding Prevention of Corruption Act offenses lies with CVC, whereas administrative control rests with the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions.
